about: Skills tool: chi-square goodness of fit. Solver and generator: ApBioProblems, kind chi. The critical value table is ApBioMath.CHI_CRIT; the validator checks it against the standard values for df 1-8 and checks every expected count is at least 5.
intro: Test whether observed counts fit what a hypothesis predicts. Work out the expected counts, the chi-square value and the degrees of freedom, find the critical value in the table, and decide about the null hypothesis.
howItWorks:
χ² = Σ (o − e)² / e

  • o is each observed count; e is the count expected if the null hypothesis is true: the total number counted × the expected fraction for that category.
  • Degrees of freedom = number of categories − 1.
  • Compare χ² with the critical value for your degrees of freedom at p = 0.05 (the table on this page). If χ² is larger, reject the null hypothesis: a difference this large would happen by chance less than 5% of the time. If it is smaller, fail to reject the null: chance could explain the difference. Failing to reject is not proof that the null is true.
  • Use counts, never percentages, and every expected count should be at least 5 for the test to be reliable.
  • Expected counts and χ² count when within one unit of the last decimal place asked for, or within 1%. Degrees of freedom must be exact; the critical value must match the table (for df 3, 7.81 and 7.82 both count).

explore.refHtml:
What the test asks

The null hypothesis says the bugs have no preference, so every chamber expects the same count: the total ÷ the number of chambers. χ² = Σ (o − e)² / e adds up how far each observed count (o) is from its expected count (e). A count that is too low adds to χ² just as much as one that is too high.

The decision

Degrees of freedom (df) = number of categories − 1. Find the critical value for that df in the p = 0.05 row of the formula sheet table. If χ² is greater than the critical value, reject the null hypothesis: a gap that big would happen by chance less than 5% of the time if the null were true. Otherwise fail to reject the null hypothesis: chance could explain the gap. Failing to reject is not proof that the null is true, and rejecting it does not say why the bugs went where they did.

Let them wander

Each bug picks a chamber at random with equal chance, so the null is true. Each run is a dot over its χ². The dots pile up into the shape of the curve, and about 1 run in 20 lands past the critical value: that 5% is the chance of a false alarm (a type I error). Bugs come in whole numbers, so the real chance is near 5% but not exactly 5% (about 4% for 40 bugs in two chambers, about 6% for 80); the curve is the smooth version the table comes from.

Good practice

Use counts, never percentages, and every expected count should be at least 5. More bugs give the same lean a bigger χ², so a big sample can detect a small preference.
